body_es: La validación de datos antes de entrenar un modelo comprueba que el conjunto cumple reglas de completitud, unicidad y rango antes de que un valor corrupto se propague al pipeline de features. En AWS Glue Data Quality esas reglas se escriben con Data Quality Definition Language: IsComplete sobre un campo exige que ninguna fila tenga null en esa columna, IsUnique exige que no haya duplicados, y expresiones como Mean entre dos valores o ColumnValues con una lista permitida y un umbral de tolerancia permiten aceptar un porcentaje de excepciones en lugar de exigir un cumplimiento absoluto. Las reglas se combinan con operadores and y or entre paréntesis para formar reglas compuestas, y se agrupan en un ruleset que corre como parte del job de ETL o directamente sobre una tabla del Data Catalog. Por ejemplo, sobre un lote de pedidos con un campo amount vacío, un order_id duplicado y un importe negativo, calcular a mano la completitud de amount, la unicidad de order_id y el porcentaje de valores dentro de un rango válido reproduce exactamente lo que evaluarían una regla de completitud, una de unicidad y una de rango sobre esa misma tabla. Un error común es fijar un umbral de completitud demasiado laxo, por ejemplo aceptar un 70% de completitud en un campo que alimenta directamente una feature del modelo: la regla nunca falla en producción, pero ese 30% de filas con null llega al entrenamiento convertido en ceros o en la media de la columna, sesgando las predicciones sin que ninguna alerta lo detecte.
body_en: Data validation before training a model checks that a dataset satisfies completeness, uniqueness, and range rules before a corrupted value can propagate into the feature pipeline. AWS Glue Data Quality expresses those rules in the Data Quality Definition Language: an IsComplete rule on a field requires that no row hold a null in that column, an IsUnique rule requires no duplicate values, and expressions such as a Mean bounded between two numbers or a ColumnValues rule constrained to an allowed list with a tolerance threshold let you accept a percentage of exceptions instead of demanding perfect compliance. Rules combine through and/or operators wrapped in parentheses to build composite rules, and they get grouped into a ruleset that runs as part of an ETL job or directly against a Data Catalog table. As a concrete case, given a batch of orders with an empty amount field, a duplicated order_id, and a negative amount, computing by hand the completeness of amount, the uniqueness of order_id, and the share of values inside a valid range reproduces exactly what a completeness rule, a uniqueness rule, and a range rule would evaluate on that same table. A common mistake is setting a completeness threshold too loosely, for instance accepting 70% completeness on a field that feeds a model feature directly: the rule never fails in production, yet that remaining 30% of null rows reaches training turned into zeros or into the column's mean, biasing predictions with no alert ever catching it.
example_code:
records = [
    {"order_id": "o1", "amount": 42.5, "customer": "ada@example.com"},
    {"order_id": "o2", "amount": None, "customer": "ada@example.com"},
    {"order_id": "o3", "amount": 15.0, "customer": None},
    {"order_id": "o4", "amount": -3.0, "customer": "grace@example.com"},
    {"order_id": "o1", "amount": 42.5, "customer": "ada@example.com"},
]

def completeness(records, field):
    present = sum(1 for r in records if r.get(field) is not None)
    return present / len(records)

def uniqueness(records, field):
    values = [r[field] for r in records]
    return len(set(values)) / len(values)

def valid_range(records, field, low, high):
    valid = sum(1 for r in records if r.get(field) is not None and low <= r[field] <= high)
    total = sum(1 for r in records if r.get(field) is not None)
    return valid / total

print(f"completeness(amount) = {completeness(records, 'amount'):.2f}")
print(f"completeness(customer) = {completeness(records, 'customer'):.2f}")
print(f"uniqueness(order_id) = {uniqueness(records, 'order_id'):.2f}")
print(f"valid_range(amount, 0, 1000) = {valid_range(records, 'amount', 0, 1000):.2f}")
source: AWS Documentation — Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) reference (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/dqdl.html)
